title: Galvani, Volta, and animal electricity
text:
CHAPTER 2. ELECTRICITY AND THE NERVE
SECTION 2.1. GALVANI, VOLTA, AND ANIMAL ELECTRICITY

The problem to be solved

By the middle of the eighteenth century, the hydraulic theory of nerve action was in trouble. Muscles did not swell with fluid when they contracted, and no one could find the hollow channels in nerves that the theory required. Yet nerves clearly carried some kind of influence very rapidly from the brain to the muscles. What was it?

At the same time, electricity had become one of the most exciting topics in natural philosophy. The Leyden jar, a simple capacitor, was invented in the mid-1740s (associated with Ewald Georg von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek), and it allowed experimenters to store charge and deliver dramatic shocks. Benjamin Franklin's experiments in the 1740s and 1750s, including the kite experiment associated with him, linked lightning to electricity. Electrostatic generators made from rotating glass globes or plates were common in laboratories and even in salons, where people demonstrated shocks for entertainment.

People noticed that electric shocks made muscles twitch. Some physicians tried electric shocks as therapy for paralysis. There were also well known "electric fish," such as the torpedo ray and the electric eel, which could deliver shocks; in the 1770s John Walsh and others showed that the torpedo's shock was electrical. So the idea that animals might produce or use electricity was in the air. The question was whether electricity was the actual agent of nerve conduction in ordinary animals, not just in special electric fish.

Luigi Galvani

Luigi Galvani (1737 to 1798) was a physician and anatomist in Bologna, a professor at the university there, and a member of the Academy of Sciences of the Bologna Institute. Beginning in the 1780s, he carried out a long series of experiments on frogs, often working together with his wife, Lucia Galeazzi, who came from a scientific family, and with his nephew Giovanni Aldini. Galvani's main publication on the topic was De viribus electricitatis in motu musculari commentarius ("Commentary on the effects of electricity on muscular motion"), published in 1791.

The frog preparation

Galvani's standard preparation was the frog's legs, attached to a section of spinal cord by the crural nerves (the large nerves running to the legs). Frogs were convenient because their muscles continue to respond for a long time after the animal is killed and dissected. Galvani often attached a metal wire or hook to the spinal cord.

Galvani's key observations, simplified, were these:

1. Spark at a distance. When an electrostatic machine was discharged somewhere in the room, a dissected frog leg nearby, touched with a metal scalpel at its nerve, could twitch. The spark did not touch the frog; the effect seems to have been caused by the electrical disturbance of the spark inducing a small current in the metal touching the nerve. This showed that the nerve-muscle preparation was an extremely sensitive detector of electricity.

2. Atmospheric electricity. Galvani hung frog preparations on metal hooks attached to an iron railing outdoors during thunderstorms and saw contractions associated with lightning. This connected the frog response to natural atmospheric electricity.

3. Metal arcs. Galvani then noticed that frog legs hanging from brass hooks on an iron railing sometimes twitched even on calm days without storms. He brought the experiment indoors and found that if he made a circuit connecting the nerve and the muscle with two different metals in contact (for example, a brass hook in the spinal cord pressed against an iron plate that touched the leg), the muscle contracted. Contractions could occur with a single metal too, though they were generally stronger with two different metals.

Galvani's interpretation: animal electricity

Galvani concluded that the electricity came from the animal itself. In his view, muscles behaved like Leyden jars, with an inner and outer surface holding opposite charges, and the nerve served as a conductor that, when a circuit was completed, allowed the stored "animal electricity" to discharge and trigger contraction. The metals in his experiments, he thought, merely provided a conductive path, closing the circuit.

This interpretation was revolutionary. It meant the nerve's mysterious agent was electricity generated within living tissue. It replaced the animal spirits with something physical and measurable.

Alessandro Volta's objection

Alessandro Volta (1745 to 1827), professor of physics at the University of Pavia, initially accepted Galvani's work and repeated the experiments. But he soon came to a different interpretation. Volta noticed that the effect depended strongly on using two different metals. He proposed that the electricity was generated by the contact of the dissimilar metals, not by the animal. The frog, in his view, was just a very sensitive electroscope, a detector, and the wet tissue served as a conductor between the metals.

Volta tested this idea using his own body as a detector as well. For example, he placed two different metals on and under his tongue, connected them, and noticed a sour or bitter taste. He also explored the effect on the eye, where a sensation of light could be produced. These observations supported the idea that the source was the metal junction and the moist conductor between, not any special property of frog tissue.

The Galvani-Volta controversy

The debate that followed is one of the most instructive controversies in the history of science, because both sides were partly right.

Galvani and his supporters, especially Aldini, looked for experiments that eliminated the metals entirely. In one important experiment, published in the 1790s (the experiment is often credited to Galvani in an anonymous publication of 1794, though the exact authorship and dates of individual experiments are discussed in the historical literature), a contraction was produced simply by bringing the cut end of one nerve into contact with the muscle, or by bringing the cut nerve of one leg into contact with the other leg, with no metal at all. Since there was no metal junction, Volta's explanation could not apply. This was strong evidence that animal tissue itself could be a source of electricity. We would now say that the injured end of a nerve or muscle is at a different potential from intact tissue, so that touching them together produces a current (the "injury current" or "demarcation potential").

Volta, meanwhile, pursued his contact theory and in doing so made one of the most important inventions in history. Around 1799 he built a stack of alternating discs of two different metals (for example, zinc and silver or copper) separated by pieces of cardboard or cloth soaked in salt water. This "voltaic pile," announced in a letter to the Royal Society of London in 1800, produced a continuous electric current, unlike the brief discharge of a Leyden jar. It was the first electric battery. Volta was explicitly inspired by the electric organs of fish, and he described his pile as an "artificial electric organ."

So Volta was right that dissimilar metals in an electrolyte generate electricity, which explained many of the original frog experiments. And Galvani was right that animal tissue generates electricity, which was demonstrated by the experiments without metals. For a while Volta's view seemed to win, partly because the battery was so obviously important, and partly because Galvani's evidence was subtle. Galvani lost his university position in the late 1790s after refusing to swear allegiance to the new Cisalpine Republic established under Napoleonic influence, and he died in 1798. Proper vindication of animal electricity came in the nineteenth century, when instruments became sensitive enough to measure the small currents directly, as we will see in the next section.

Aldini and the public spectacle

Giovanni Aldini, Galvani's nephew, promoted animal electricity energetically, including in public demonstrations on the bodies of executed criminals, using voltaic piles to make the faces and limbs of corpses move. The best known of these was in London in 1803, using the body of a man named George Forster, who had been hanged at Newgate. These demonstrations were sensational and are often mentioned as part of the cultural background to Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818), in which a body is brought to life by an unspecified scientific method; Shelley herself referred to galvanism in her introduction to the 1831 edition. The word "galvanize," meaning to shock into action, comes from Galvani's name.

The engineering view: sensors and sources

The Galvani-Volta controversy is, at heart, a measurement problem: is the observed signal generated by the system under test, or by the measurement apparatus? Every engineer who has dealt with a thermocouple has faced this. A thermocouple works precisely because junctions of dissimilar metals generate a voltage that depends on temperature (the Seebeck effect). If you connect a sensitive amplifier to a biological sample with dissimilar metal electrodes in salty fluid, you will get electrochemical potentials at the electrode-electrolyte interfaces that have nothing to do with the biology. Modern electrophysiologists deal with this using non-polarizable electrodes, such as silver/silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) electrodes, which minimize junction potentials and drift, and by careful use of reference electrodes and controls.

So Volta's objection, which seemed to undercut Galvani, was in fact a correct identification of an artifact. Galvani's response, eliminating the metal entirely, was the right control experiment. Good science involves both sides: identifying artifacts and designing experiments that rule them out.

What was actually happening in Galvani's frogs?

With modern knowledge, we can interpret Galvani's observations:

- Nerve and muscle cells maintain a voltage across their membranes, the inside being negative relative to the outside by tens of millivolts. This "resting potential" is maintained by ion pumps and selective ion channels, as we will see in section 2.3.
- When a nerve fiber is stimulated sufficiently, its membrane voltage changes rapidly, producing an action potential that travels along the fiber. When the action potential reaches the muscle, it triggers chemical transmission at the neuromuscular junction, which leads to muscle action potentials and contraction.
- An external current, whether from a spark, a battery, or a junction of dissimilar metals, can depolarize the nerve membrane and trigger action potentials. This explains the contractions in experiments with metals.
- The cut end of a nerve or muscle has lost its membrane barrier, so its interior potential is exposed. Touching it to intact tissue allows current to flow between regions at different potentials, which can stimulate the nerve. This explains the contractions without metals.

So the nerve impulse is electrical, but it is not simply electricity flowing down a wire like current in copper. Nerves are poor passive conductors. As we will see, the impulse is a self-regenerating wave of membrane voltage change, powered locally along the fiber by ionic gradients. Understanding that difference took more than a century and a half after Galvani.

Bridge to AI: signals, spikes, and the birth of the analog neuron

Galvani's discovery established that neural signals are electrical. This is the fact that makes the whole comparison between brains and computers possible. Every model of a neuron that you will encounter, from the McCulloch-Pitts logic unit to modern spiking neuron models, starts from the idea that neurons are electrical devices that receive inputs, combine them, and produce outputs.

In artificial neural networks, a "neuron" takes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a nonlinear function, such as the sigmoid or the rectified linear unit (ReLU). This is a drastic abstraction of the electrical events Galvani first glimpsed. The threshold-like behavior of a frog nerve, where a weak stimulus does nothing and a strong enough stimulus produces a full response, is the biological root of the nonlinear activation function. In Galvani's frogs, too weak a spark produced no twitch, while a stronger one produced a twitch. That simple threshold nonlinearity, as later work would show, is a key ingredient that gives networks their computational power: without nonlinearities, a stack of layers collapses into a single linear transformation.

There is also a hardware connection. Volta's battery, inspired by an electric fish, launched electrical engineering. Two centuries later, engineers are trying to build "neuromorphic" chips that compute with brief electrical spikes, like neurons, to save energy compared with conventional processors. The line from Galvani's frog legs to spiking neuromorphic hardware is long, but it is direct.

Summary

- In the eighteenth century, electricity became a major research topic, and electric fish showed that animals could produce electric shocks.
- Luigi Galvani in Bologna showed that frog legs contract in response to electrical sparks, atmospheric electricity, and circuits made of metals, and he proposed that animals generate their own "animal electricity" (published 1791).
- Alessandro Volta argued that the electricity came from contact between dissimilar metals, and in developing this idea he invented the voltaic pile (announced 1800), the first battery.
- Experiments without metals supported Galvani's view that living tissue produces electricity, while Volta was right that metal junctions produce electricity.
- The controversy is a classic case of distinguishing signal from measurement artifact.
- Galvani's discovery that neural signals are electrical underlies all later models of neurons, biological and artificial.
